definition.text: The quantitative property transferred to a body or system, seen in the capacity to do work and in heat and light.

facts.text: Energy is conserved: the total energy of an isolated system stays constant, though it can change form.
The first law of thermodynamics says a closed system's energy is constant unless transferred in or out as work or heat.
The SI unit is the joule, the work done by one newton over one metre; power, energy per unit time, is measured in watts, one joule per second.
Total energy divides into potential and kinetic energy, and forms such as mechanical or nuclear energy are combinations of the two.
In irreversible processes energy is dissipated into available states and cannot be recovered into more concentrated forms without degrading more energy.
Living things need an external energy source: sunlight for green plants, chemical energy for animals; cellular respiration stores energy in carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.
Sunlight is the main input to Earth's energy budget, which accounts for its temperature and climate stability.
